slides.headline: THE QUESTION THAT ENDS INTERVIEWS
slides.body: Any questions for us? Ask these instead.

slides.headline: YOUR QUESTIONS GET SCORED TOO
slides.body: The last five minutes are the last thing they remember. One lazy question can undo a strong hour.

slides.headline: NEVER ASK WHAT THEY DO
slides.body: Read their site and one recent news item. Then ask about it.

left.title: SINKS YOU
lines: So, what does your company do?

right.title: ASK INSTEAD
lines: You just launched in Pune. How does this role support that?

slides.headline: SALARY AND WFH COME LATER
slides.body: Fair questions, wrong moment. Asked first, they sound like all you want.

items: The work, the team, the goals

slides.headline: DON'T ASK IF YOU GOT IT
slides.body: They usually can't answer yet. Ask for the timeline instead.

lines: When should I expect to hear?
a date you can follow up on

slides.headline: DON'T JUMP TO PROMOTION
slides.body: Ask what great looks like in year one. Same ambition, better signal.

slides.headline: NEVER HAVE ZERO QUESTIONS
slides.body: "No, you covered it all" reads as low interest. Bring three in case two get answered.

items: What does success look like at 90 days?
What's the hardest part of this role?
What do your best people do differently?

visual.text: Is there anything in my background that makes you hesitate?
visual.who: lets you answer a doubt while you're still in the room

slides.headline: THE END-OF-INTERVIEW RULES
items: Ask about year one, not promotion

slides.headline: SAVE THIS
slides.body: Read it the night before your next interview.

caption:
One question in the last 5 minutes can undo a 45-minute interview: "So, what does your company do?"

It happens right after they ask if you have any questions for them. Most people treat that bit as a formality. Wrong. Interviewers write down what you ask, and your interview questions get read as closely as your answers.

The ones that hurt are ordinary. Asking what the company does when their LinkedIn page and last 3 press releases are one search away. Opening with salary, 24 days of leave or 2 WFH days. "Did I get it?" while 4 other candidates are still booked that week. Asking about promotion before day 1.

Pay and remote work are fair to ask about. Just later, with the recruiter or at the offer stage.

Ask about the work instead. What does success look like at 90 days? What's the hardest part of this role? My favourite of all the questions to ask the interviewer is the closer: is there anything in my background that makes you hesitate? You get to fix the doubt while you're still in the room, not in an email 2 days later.

Save this for the night before your next interview.
